chapterTitle: Friendship with the World, and the Grace Given to the Humble
themeTitle: “Draw Near to God, and He Will Draw Near to You”

scripture.text: Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?
scripture.understanding: πόθεν πόλεμοι καὶ πόθεν μάχαι ἐν ὑμῖν, “Where do wars and fightings among you come from?” — πόλεμος, a war, a long campaign; μάχη, a battle, a single fight. Church conflict described in military language. James answers with a question: ἐκ τῶν ἡδονῶν ὑμῶν, “from your pleasures” — ἡδονή, pleasure, the root of ‘hedonism’ — τῶν στρατευομένων ἐν τοῖς μέλεσιν ὑμῶν, “that war in your members.” The war outside starts with a war inside.

scripture.text: You lust, and don’t have. You murder and covet, and can’t obtain. You fight and make war. You don’t have, because you don’t ask.
scripture.understanding: “You lust, and don’t have.” ἐπιθυμέω, to set the heart on. “You murder and covet” — φονεύω and ζηλόω: jealous desire that leads to destroying others, whether literally or, as Jesus taught, by hatred in the heart. ἐπιτυχεῖν, to obtain. “You fight and make war” — μάχομαι and πολεμέω, the verbs of verse 1. And the tragic irony: “You don’t have, because you don’t ask” — αἰτέω, from the pray family. They grab instead of asking.

scripture.text: You ask, and don’t receive, because you ask with wrong motives, so that you may spend it on your pleasures.
scripture.understanding: “You ask, and don’t receive” — αἰτέω again, from the pray family. When they do pray, they pray κακῶς, “with wrong motives” — from the evil family: the adverb of κακός, badly. ἵνα ἐν ταῖς ἡδοναῖς ὑμῶν δαπανήσητε, “so that you may spend it on your pleasures” — δαπανάω, to spend, to squander, as the prodigal son spent everything. They treat God as a supplier for their desires.

scripture.text: You adulterers and adulteresses, don’t you know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God? Whoever therefore wants to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God.
scripture.understanding: μοιχαλίδες, “You adulterers and adulteresses” — the oldest manuscripts read only μοιχαλίδες, ‘adulteresses’, the language of the prophets for God's people, His bride, being unfaithful (Hosea 3:1). The WEB follows manuscripts that add the masculine. ἡ φιλία τοῦ κόσμου ἔχθρα τοῦ θεοῦ ἐστιν, “friendship with the world is hostility toward God” — φιλία, from the love family: warm affection and loyalty; κόσμος, from the world family: society organised without God, not the created earth (γῆ). ἔχθρα, hostility. “Whoever therefore wants to be a friend of the world” — φίλος, the word used of Abraham, the friend of God (2:23) — “makes himself an enemy of God.” You cannot be a friend of both.

scripture.text: Or do you think that the Scripture says in vain, “The Spirit who lives in us yearns jealously”?
scripture.understanding: “Or do you think that the Scripture says in vain” — κενῶς, emptily. “The Spirit who lives in us yearns jealously” — no Old Testament verse says these exact words; James is summarising Scripture's teaching about God's jealous love. The Greek can be read two ways: ‘God jealously yearns for the spirit He made to live in us’ (the jealousy of a faithful husband for his bride, Exodus 34:14), or ‘the spirit that lives in us yearns enviously’ (the human spirit's sinful desires). The flow from verse 4, ‘adulteresses’, and verse 6, ‘he gives more grace’, favours the first: God loves His people with a jealous love and will not share them. ἐπιποθέω, to long for intensely; φθόνος, jealousy.

scripture.text: But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”
scripture.understanding: μείζονα δὲ δίδωσιν χάριν, “But he gives more grace” — greater grace: grace greater than the world's pull and God's jealousy combined. The proof text is Proverbs 3:34 in the Greek Old Testament, which Peter also quotes: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” ἀντιτάσσεται, from the resist family: a military word, to draw up battle lines against. ὑπερήφανος, proud — literally ‘appearing above’ others. ταπεινός, from the humble family: low. God fights the proud and floods the humble with grace.

scripture.text: Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
scripture.understanding: ὑποτάγητε οὖν τῷ θεῷ, “Be subject therefore to God” — ὑποτάσσω, to rank yourself under: surrender, the opposite of pride. Then, ἀντίστητε δὲ τῷ διαβόλῳ, “Resist the devil” — ἀνθίστημι, the second word of the resist family: stand your ground against an attack. God ἀντιτάσσεται the proud (v. 6); you ἀνθίστημι the devil. καὶ φεύξεται ἀφ᾽ ὑμῶν, “and he will flee from you” — φεύγω, to run away. The devil is not stronger than a submitted believer.

scripture.text: Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners; and purify your hearts, you double-minded.
scripture.understanding: ἐγγίσατε τῷ θεῷ, καὶ ἐγγιεῖ ὑμῖν, “Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you” — ἐγγίζω, the priestly word for approaching God, which Hebrews uses for drawing near through Christ (Hebrews 7:19). “Cleanse your hands, you sinners” — καθαρίζω, the outward life; ἁμαρτωλός, from the sin family: those whose lives are marked by sin. “and purify your hearts, you double-minded” — ἁγνίζω, the inward life; δίψυχος, the two-souled person of 1:8. Hands and heart, deeds and desires, both made clean.

scripture.text: Lament, mourn, and weep. Let your laughter be turned to mourning, and your joy to gloom.
scripture.understanding: ταλαιπωρήσατε καὶ πενθήσατε καὶ κλαύσατε, “Lament, mourn, and weep” — ταλαιπωρέω, to feel your wretchedness; πενθέω, to grieve as for the dead; κλαίω, to weep aloud. “Let your laughter be turned to mourning” — γέλως, the careless laughter of people who do not take sin seriously, as in Jesus' woe on those who laugh now. “and your joy to gloom” — κατήφεια, a downcast face, eyes lowered in shame. This is not a command to be miserable forever, but to grieve over sin until it is gone.

scripture.text: Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you.
scripture.understanding: ταπεινώθητε ἐνώπιον κυρίου, “Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord” — ταπεινόω, from the humble family: take the low place, before His face. καὶ ὑψώσει ὑμᾶς, “and he will exalt you” — ὑψόω, to lift high. The humbled poor man of 1:9 boasts in his ὕψος. God lifts those who bow; Jesus said the same, and lived it (Philippians 2:8–9).

scripture.text: Don’t speak against one another, brothers. He who speaks against a brother and judges his brother, speaks against the law and judges the law. But if you judge the law, you are not a doer of the law, but a judge.
scripture.understanding: μὴ καταλαλεῖτε ἀλλήλων, “Don’t speak against one another, brothers” — καταλαλέω, to talk down, to slander. This is the tongue of chapter 3 again. “He who speaks against a brother and judges his brother, speaks against the law and judges the law” — the royal law says love your neighbour (2:8); to slander him is to say that law does not apply to you. “But if you judge the law, you are not a doer of the law, but a judge” — ποιητής, the ‘doer’ of 1:22; κριτής, the ‘judge’ of 2:4. You have climbed onto the bench.

scripture.text: Only one is the lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy. But who are you to judge another?
scripture.understanding: εἷς ἐστιν ὁ νομοθέτης καὶ κριτής, “Only one is the lawgiver” — νομοθέτης, legislator. ὁ δυνάμενος σῶσαι καὶ ἀπολέσαι, “who is able to save and to destroy” — σῴζω, from the heal family, to rescue and make whole; δύναμαι, from the power family: the capability to act, as distinct from ἐξουσία (the authority) or κράτος (sheer might). Only God has the power to decide a person's eternity. “But who are you to judge another?” — τὸν πλησίον, your neighbour: the one the royal law commands you to love.

scripture.text: Come now, you who say, “Today or tomorrow let’s go into this city, and spend a year there, trade, and make a profit.”
scripture.understanding: ἄγε νῦν, “Come now” — a sharp call to attention. “Today or tomorrow let’s go into this city, and spend a year there, trade, and make a profit.” Three words from the time family: σήμερον, today; αὔριον, tomorrow; ἐνιαυτός, a year. They plan the when, the where, the how long and the profit — everything except God. ἐμπορεύομαι, to travel as a merchant; κερδαίνω, to gain.

scripture.text: Whereas you don’t know what your life will be like tomorrow. For what is your life? For you are a vapor, that appears for a little time, and then vanishes away.
scripture.understanding: οἵτινες οὐκ ἐπίστασθε τὸ τῆς αὔριον, “Whereas you don’t know what your life will be like tomorrow” — αὔριον, from the time family; ἐπίσταμαι, from the know family: to know as an expert knows, to understand; you are no expert on tomorrow. “For what is your life?” — ζωή, from the life family. ἀτμὶς γάρ ἐστε, “For you are a vapor” — ἀτμίς, a puff of steam or smoke, breath on a cold morning. Then a wordplay from the appear family: ἡ … φαινομένη, ἔπειτα καὶ ἀφανιζομένη, “that appears for a little time, and then vanishes away” — φαίνω, to appear, and ἀφανίζω, to disappear. ‘Time’ is added by the translators; the Greek simply says ‘for a little’.

scripture.text: For you ought to say, “If the Lord wills, we will both live, and do this or that.”
scripture.understanding: “For you ought to say, ‘If the Lord wills, we will both live, and do this or that.’” ἐὰν ὁ κύριος θελήσῃ — θέλω, to will, to decide. Not a magic phrase to add to plans, but a humble heart behind them. ζάω, from the life family: even staying alive is up to Him. Paul used the same words: “I will return again to you if God wills” (Acts 18:21).

scripture.text: But now you glory in your boasting. All such boasting is evil.
scripture.understanding: “But now you glory in your boasting” — καυχάομαι, the ‘glory’ of 1:9, now misused; ἀλαζονεία, arrogant pretension, the swagger of someone claiming more than he has. “All such boasting is evil” — καύχησις, boasting; πονηρός, from the evil family: actively harmful, and in the singular the word used for ‘the evil one’. Boasting about tomorrow sides with him.

scripture.text: To him therefore who knows to do good, and doesn’t do it, to him it is sin.
scripture.understanding: εἰδότι οὖν καλὸν ποιεῖν καὶ μὴ ποιοῦντι, ἁμαρτία αὐτῷ ἐστιν, “To him therefore who knows to do good, and doesn’t do it, to him it is sin.” εἴδω, from the know family (and the see family, since its root means ‘to see’): to know the facts; καλός, from the good family: the fine and fitting thing; ἁμαρτία, from the sin family. Sin is not only doing wrong but failing to do right — the sin of omission. The whole letter in one verse: hearing and knowing without doing is sin.

visualMeditations.title: The War Inside
visualMeditations.image: Picture a church business meeting that has turned into a battlefield. Voices are raised; two factions glare across the room; people who once prayed together now refuse to speak. Then picture a camera zooming in — past the faces, past the words — into each person's chest, where another war is raging: wants fighting wants, pride fighting pride, desire grabbing for what it cannot have.
visualMeditations.meaning: “Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?” (v. 1). The fights outside begin with the fights inside. James's answer is not to win the argument but to change the desire. And he adds a quiet rebuke: “You don’t have, because you don’t ask” (v. 2). What we grab for by fighting, God would often have given if we had asked.

visualMeditations.title: The Unfaithful Bride
visualMeditations.image: Picture a wedding ring left on a bedside table in a stranger's house. A wife has slipped away from her husband, who has loved her faithfully, to spend the night with someone who promises excitement and flattery. At home the husband waits by the window, grieving — not with cold anger, but with a jealous, aching love.
visualMeditations.meaning: “You adulterers and adulteresses, don’t you know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God?” (v. 4). God's people are His bride. To love the world's values, pleasures and approval is spiritual adultery. And God's response is not indifference but jealousy: “The Spirit who lives in us yearns jealously” (v. 5). He wants all of you. And He offers more grace to bring you home.

visualMeditations.title: The Devil in Retreat
visualMeditations.image: Picture a soldier standing alone on a hill, his armour on, his sword drawn, his feet planted. Across the valley an enemy army approaches, roaring and confident. But the soldier does not move; behind him stands his King. The enemy reaches the foot of the hill, sees who stands with him — and turns and runs.
visualMeditations.meaning: “Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (v. 7). The order matters: first submit, then resist. The devil does not flee from the proud, who stand alone, but from the humble, who stand under God. “Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you” (v. 8). Your strength in spiritual warfare is your nearness to God.

visualMeditations.title: The Morning Mist
visualMeditations.image: Picture a cold morning in the hills. A merchant steps out of his house with his travel plans and his money bag, and his breath hangs in the air like a small white cloud. For a moment it is clearly visible. Then the sun rises over the hill, and the cloud is gone, and the valley mist with it. By noon no one could tell it was ever there.
visualMeditations.meaning: “For what is your life? For you are a vapor, that appears for a little time, and then vanishes away” (v. 14). Making plans is not wrong. Making them as if you controlled tomorrow is. “For you ought to say, ‘If the Lord wills, we will both live, and do this or that’” (v. 15). Every plan you make should be held in an open hand.

structure.label: The Source of Conflict (v. 1-3)
structure.body: Fights and quarrels come from desires at war within; people covet, murder and fight because they do not ask God, or they ask wrongly, to spend on their pleasures.

structure.label: Spiritual Adultery and Greater Grace (v. 4-6)
structure.body: Friendship with the world is hostility to God; God yearns jealously over His people and gives more grace, opposing the proud and giving grace to the humble.

structure.label: The Call to Return (v. 7-10)
structure.body: Submit to God, resist the devil and he will flee; draw near to God and He will draw near; cleanse hands and purify hearts; mourn over sin; humble yourselves before the Lord and He will lift you up.

structure.label: Do Not Judge (v. 11-12)
structure.body: Speaking against a brother is judging the law instead of doing it; there is only one Lawgiver and Judge, who can save and destroy.

structure.label: Do Not Boast About Tomorrow (v. 13-17)
structure.body: Those who plan trade and profit without God do not know what tomorrow holds, for life is a vapour; they should say, ‘If the Lord wills’; boasting is evil, and knowing the good and not doing it is sin.

sections.heading: Where Quarrels Come From
paragraphs: James 3 ended with peace: “Now the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace” (James 3:18). James 4 begins with war. The believers were fighting — perhaps over position, money, leadership or doctrine — and James goes straight to the root: “Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?” (v. 1). Paul describes the same inner battle: “For the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh” (Galatians 5:17). When desires rule the heart, they will eventually fight other people's desires.

James traces the chain in verse 2: desire, frustration, violence. “You lust, and don’t have. You murder and covet, and can’t obtain.” The word ‘murder’ may be literal — some Jewish zealots of the time did kill for their cause — or it may be Jesus' sense, that hatred is murder in the heart. Either way, the result is war. And underneath it all is prayerlessness: “You don’t have, because you don’t ask” (v. 2). Or, when they do pray, their prayers are only another way of feeding the same desires: “You ask, and don’t receive, because you ask with wrong motives, so that you may spend it on your pleasures” (v. 3).

This is a searching diagnosis. Many church fights are not really about the issue on the table. They are about wanting, not getting, and refusing to take the want to God in honest prayer. The way out is not a better strategy but a changed heart — and that is where James goes next.

sections.heading: Friendship with the World and the Jealous Love of God
paragraphs: James's language now becomes shocking: “You adulterers and adulteresses” (v. 4). He is using the prophets' picture of Israel as God's unfaithful wife. To be a ‘friend of the world’ is not to love the world of people God loves (John 3:16), but to embrace the world's system of values — its pride, greed, lust and self-promotion. John says the same: “Don’t love the world or the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the Father’s love isn’t in him” (1 John 2:15), “For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s” (1 John 2:16). James makes it starker: friendship with one is enmity with the other.

Verse 5 is one of the hardest verses in the letter. The words “The Spirit who lives in us yearns jealously” are not found word for word in the Old Testament, and the Greek can mean either that God jealously longs for the spirit He placed in us, or that the human spirit within us has envious longings. Both are true, but the context — spiritual adultery before it and greater grace after it — points to God's jealous love. God is not a casual partner. He loves His people with the burning, exclusive love of a faithful husband. That is not a threat but a comfort: He will not give you up.

And then comes the turning point of the chapter: “But he gives more grace” (v. 6). Whatever the world's pull, God's grace is greater. But that grace flows in only one direction: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (v. 6). Pride does not just miss grace; it turns God into an opponent. Humility does not earn grace; it opens the door to it.

sections.heading: Ten Commands for the Way Back
paragraphs: Verses 7–10 contain ten commands in a row, all calling for urgent action: submit, resist, draw near, cleanse, purify, lament, mourn, weep, turn, humble yourselves. It is a call to repentance. It begins with surrender — “Be subject therefore to God” — and ends with surrender — “Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you” (v. 10). Between them is the battle: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (v. 7). Peter says the same: “Withstand him steadfast in your faith” (1 Peter 5:9).

The promise of verse 8 is one of the most precious in Scripture: “Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you.” God does not wait at a distance with folded arms. The moment you turn towards Him, He comes towards you, like the father running to the prodigal. But drawing near requires clean hands (what you do) and a pure heart (what you want). The double-minded person of 1:8 must become single-hearted. Hebrews gives the way: “let’s draw near with a true heart in fullness of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience” (Hebrews 10:22).

The call to mourn (v. 9) is not a call to permanent sadness. It is a call to take sin seriously, as Jesus said: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew 5:4). Grief over sin is the doorway to joy. And verse 10 sums up the whole gospel pattern. Jesus Himself lived it: “he humbled himself, becoming obedient to death, yes, the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:8), and “Therefore God also highly exalted him” (Philippians 2:9). The way up is down.

sections.heading: Judging Others and Boasting About Tomorrow
paragraphs: Two forms of pride close the chapter. The first is judging others: “Don’t speak against one another, brothers” (v. 11). To slander a brother is to set yourself above the law of love, as if it did not apply to you. “Only one is the lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy. But who are you to judge another?” (v. 12). Jesus said, “Don’t judge, so that you won’t be judged” (Matthew 7:1), and Paul asks, “But you, why do you judge your brother?” (Romans 14:10). Discernment is needed in the church, but condemning, gossiping and tearing down are not discernment. They are taking God's seat.

The second is planning without God. The merchants of verse 13 are not condemned for making business plans, but for making them as if they were in charge of time, health and success. “Whereas you don’t know what your life will be like tomorrow. For what is your life? For you are a vapor, that appears for a little time, and then vanishes away” (v. 14). Jesus told the same story of the rich fool: “‘You foolish one, tonight your soul is required of you’” (Luke 12:20). The remedy is not to stop planning but to plan humbly: “If the Lord wills, we will both live, and do this or that” (v. 15).

The chapter ends with a single verse that sums up the whole letter: “To him therefore who knows to do good, and doesn’t do it, to him it is sin” (v. 17). James will not let you hide behind knowledge. If you know what is right, the only question left is whether you will do it.

ntConnection.heading: Grace to the Humble and the Devil in Flight
paragraphs: Peter quotes the same Proverb as James, with the same application: “for ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble’” (1 Peter 5:5), and then, “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time” (1 Peter 5:6). Like James, he follows it immediately with spiritual warfare: “Your adversary, the devil, walks around like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Peter 5:8), “Withstand him steadfast in your faith” (1 Peter 5:9). Two apostles, the same order: humble yourself before God, then stand against the devil.

Jesus showed what that looks like in the wilderness. Every temptation was met with submission to God's word, and the final one with a command: “Get behind me, Satan! For it is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and you shall serve him only’” (Matthew 4:10). And the result was exactly what James promises: “Then the devil left him, and behold, angels came and served him” (Matthew 4:11). Paul gives the armour for the same fight: “Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil” (Ephesians 6:11).

Jesus' teaching on humility runs through the chapter. In the parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector, the one who prayed “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” went home justified, “for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 18:14). And in Gethsemane He prayed the perfect ‘If the Lord wills’: “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). The humble submission James calls for is the path Jesus walked first.

lexicon.insight: Strong's: “sensual delight; by implication, desire.” ἡδονή is pleasure as a ruling principle — the drive to have what feels good, the root of our word ‘hedonism’. Jesus used it of the ‘pleasures of life’ that choke the word in the parable of the sower (Luke 8:14). In James it is pictured as an army camped in your body, waging war. Pleasure in itself is God's gift; pleasure as master is a tyrant that will eventually turn you against God and other people.

Strong's: “fondness.” φιλία is warm, personal affection — the love of friends, from the love family. It is the only time the noun appears in the New Testament. James uses it deliberately: in 2:23 Abraham was called φίλος θεοῦ, the friend of God; here people are φίλοι τοῦ κόσμου, friends of the world. You can only have one best friend. The question is not whether you are religious, but whose friendship you are cultivating — whose approval, values and company you most want.

Strong's: “to range oneself against, i.e. oppose.” ἀντιτάσσομαι was used of an army drawn up in battle formation. James says God takes up that position against the proud. In the next verse he uses a different word, ἀνθίστημι, ‘to stand against’, for believers resisting the devil. This study gathers them into a new resist family. The two verses belong together: if you are proud, you are fighting God; if you are humble, God fights for you, and you can stand against the devil.

Strong's: “to make near, i.e. (reflexively) approach.” In the Greek Old Testament ἐγγίζω described priests approaching God in worship. Hebrews uses it of the better hope ‘through which we draw near to God’ (Hebrews 7:19). In James 4:8 every believer is invited to come as a priest — and God promises to come towards them. In 5:8 the same word announces that ‘the coming of the Lord is at hand.’ We draw near to Him now; He draws near to us at His return.

Strong's: “mist.” ἀτμίς is a puff of smoke or steam, the kind of vapour that rises from a cooking pot or a breath on a cold day — visible for a moment and then gone. The Hebrew idea behind it is הֶבֶל, the ‘vanity’ or ‘breath’ of Ecclesiastes. James does not use it to make life meaningless, but to make it precious and humble. Because your life is a vapour, every day is a gift to be placed in God's hands with the words ‘If the Lord wills.’

holySpiritRevelation.intro: In this chapter the Holy Spirit is calling you home — from fighting, from worldliness, from pride and from self-reliance — into His jealous love.

items.title: What Are You Fighting For?
items.body: Think of the last conflict you were in — at home, at work, at church. The Spirit asks: what did you want that you were not getting? Recognition? Control? Comfort? Being right? “Where do wars and fightings among you come from?” (v. 1). And He asks a second question: did you pray about it, or only fight about it? “You don’t have, because you don’t ask” (v. 2). Take that desire to God honestly now.

items.title: Whose Friend Are You?
items.body: The Spirit does not accuse you to push you away; He yearns jealously to draw you back. Where has friendship with the world crept in — in your entertainment, your ambitions, your spending, your values, your need for approval? “Whoever therefore wants to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God” (v. 4). He is not asking you to leave the world's people, but to stop loving the world's ways. And He promises, “But he gives more grace” (v. 6).

items.title: If the Lord Wills
items.body: What plans are you making right now — for your career, your money, your family, your ministry? Have you included God in them, or only asked Him to bless what you have already decided? “For you are a vapor, that appears for a little time, and then vanishes away” (v. 14). The Spirit invites you to open your hands and say, honestly, “If the Lord wills” (v. 15). What would change in your plans if you meant it?

audit.title: The Desire Check
audit.body: What do you want so badly that it is causing conflict in your relationships (vv. 1–2)? When did you last bring that desire to God and ask Him about it — with right motives (v. 3)?

audit.title: The Friendship Check
audit.body: Whose approval do you crave most? What would you be unwilling to give up if God asked? Are there areas where you are a ‘friend of the world’ (v. 4)?

audit.title: The Knowing-Doing Check
audit.body: What good thing do you know you should do, but have not done (v. 17)? Name it specifically — a call, an apology, a gift, a change, an act of obedience.

practices.title: Ten Steps Home
practices.body: Set aside thirty minutes this week. Read verses 7–10 slowly and turn each of the ten commands into a prayer: submit (name an area you are surrendering), resist (name a temptation and refuse it in Jesus' name), draw near (spend five minutes in silent worship), cleanse your hands (confess a specific action), purify your heart (confess a specific desire), lament and mourn (let yourself feel the weight of your sin), humble yourself (kneel if you can). End by thanking God that He draws near and lifts up the humble.

practices.title: Write ‘If the Lord Wills’ on Your Plans
practices.body: Take your diary, calendar or planning list for the coming month. Next to each major plan, write ‘If the Lord wills’ — and pray over each one, asking God to change, confirm or cancel it as He chooses. Notice which plans you feel anxious about surrendering; those are the places where you are trusting yourself more than God.

prayerReflection: “Holy God, I confess that the wars outside me often begin with the wars inside me. My desires fight for what I want, and I grab instead of asking You, or I ask with wrong motives. Forgive me. I confess the places where I have been a friend of the world and so made myself Your enemy. Thank You that You love me with a jealous love and that You give more grace. I humble myself before You now, because You oppose the proud and give grace to the humble. I submit to You. In Jesus' name I resist the devil, and I believe Your word that he will flee from me. I draw near to You, Lord, and I thank You that You draw near to me. Cleanse my hands and purify my heart; make me single-minded. Let me grieve over my sin until it is gone, and then lift me up in Your time. Keep me from speaking against my brothers and sisters and from sitting in Your judgement seat. My life is a vapour, so I place my plans in Your hands: if You will, I will live and do this or that. Whatever good I know to do, give me grace to do it today. In Jesus' name, Amen.”

storyConnections.title: Jesus in the Wilderness
storyConnections.summary: After His baptism, Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness, where He fasted forty days. The devil came with three temptations: to turn stones into bread, to throw Himself from the temple, and to gain all the kingdoms of the world by worshipping him. Each time Jesus answered with Scripture, submitting Himself to His Father's word. At last He commanded, “Get behind me, Satan!” (Matthew 4:10), and “Then the devil left him, and behold, angels came and served him” (Matthew 4:11). This is James 4:7 lived out: submit to God, resist the devil, and he will flee.

storyConnections.title: The Pharisee and the Tax Collector
storyConnections.summary: Jesus told of two men who went to the temple to pray. The Pharisee stood and thanked God that he was not like other people, listing his fasting and tithing. The tax collector stood far off, would not even look up to heaven, beat his chest and prayed, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” (Luke 18:13). Jesus said the tax collector, not the Pharisee, went home justified, “for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 18:14). The tax collector is the one who lamented, mourned and humbled himself — and received the grace God gives to the humble.

storyConnections.title: The Rich Fool
storyConnections.summary: A man's land produced a great harvest, and he planned to pull down his barns and build bigger ones. He said to himself, “Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years. Take your ease, eat, drink, be merry” (Luke 12:19). “But God said to him, ‘You foolish one, tonight your soul is required of you. The things which you have prepared—whose will they be?’” (Luke 12:20). He made every plan except the one that mattered. James's merchants are the same man: they know where they will go and what they will earn, but they do not know whether they will be alive tomorrow.
